speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
High! Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister): Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Fraser) asked what had happened to the surplus money which had been collected for relief purposes following the heavy floods in Manitoba in 1950. We all, of course, recall that a corporation had been set up by our parliament in 1953. The hon. member also wanted to know if this surplus could be used for relief purposes at this time.
In 1953, when the Canadian Disaster Relief Fund Corporation was set up by act of parliament, the surplus amounted to approximately a little less than $1| million. The legislation setting up the fund expressly provided that:
The corporation may make payments out of the fund for the purpose of meeting emergencies and needs arising in Canada from flood, fire, tempest, earthquake, pestilence or other disaster, mitigating loss and suffering caused thereby assisting in repairing damages resulting therefrom, and rehabilitating persons who have suffered injury or loss by reason thereof, when in the opinion of the corporation the implementing of such purposes is beyond the reasonable capacity of the area affected.
As of December 31, 1955, the balance of the fund was $1,337,310.83.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) asked me a question yesterday which I took as notice and to which I now wish to give the answer. This is the question, Mr. Speaker:
Can the minister give the names of the representatives of the farm organizations who took part in the agricultural marketing conference held in Ottawa on April 16, 17 and 18 and as referred to on page 2774 of Hansard of April 10, 1956?
I have the names of the members of that group, but I would like to make a correction in the question. The meeting was not a marketing conference meeting. The meeting on those three dates was a meeting of the advisory committee. The marketing conference met the following day, April 19. This committee is advisory to the minister and the agricultural prices support board. The chairman of the committee is Mr. H. H. Han-nam, president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. In addition to Mr. Hannam there are as members the deputy ministers of agriculture of the ten provinces. I think all of them were present.

Inquiries of the Ministry
In addition to Mr. Hannam there are representatives of farm organizations who have been recommended by the farm organizations as members of that committee. The recommendation is made to me as minister and they are appointed by order in council. Most of them have been members of the committee for some time, and as one withdraws from the committee a new member is appointed in his place.
The first member of that group is Erie Kitchen, Ontario, secretary of the Dairy Farmers of Canada. The second member is W. J. Parker, Manitoba, president of the Manitoba wheat pool. Mr. Parker was not present during the three days of this meeting but he is usually present. Then there is Mr. H. B. Crandlemire, the maritimes, New Brunswick potato growers; Karl Kapler, Alberta, farmers' union of Alberta; R. B. Warnica, Ontario, Ontario beef cattle producers' association; George Wright, Saskatchewan, Saskatchewan federation of agriculture. Mr. Wright was not present this year. At the time he was recommended the farmers' union operated as a member of the Saskatchewan federation of agriculture and he was satisfactory to and recommended by both organizations as their representative on the committee. Then there is J. B. Le-moine, Quebec, Catholic farmers' union, and V. E. Ellison, British Columbia, British Columbia federation of agriculture.
That makes a committee of 19 members which we think is representative of the farm organizations right across Canada, even if there is not a representative on the committee from each of the many farm organizations. As a rule there are two or three recommended by the different organizations and the selections were made to cover as nearly as possible the livestock, agricultural, dairying and fruit growers' organizations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am indeed pleased to have the opportunity to speak on this occasion in support of my leader's amendment demanding financial assistance for our municipalities. As this government pursues its wayward and merry and sinister course of greater and greater centralization of power, our municipalities have become more and more forgotten governing bodies in Canada. Yet their historic and traditional functions, honoured over the years, are well defined and have been well established in the history of this country. The duties of our municipal governing bodies increase from year to year,

but as these duties increase steadily and continually, bringing in their train ever-increasing financial burdens, the necessary finances to meet these burdens become harder and harder to obtain.
It is apparent lor all to see, and we all know, that our municipal bodies-our counties, our cities, our towns, our villages, our local improvement districts, our school commissions-fulfil functions and duties of government which at the local level overshadow in importance many of the needs of those foreign nations which Canada has been anxious to gratify. In saying this I hasten to add, lest my Liberal friendly enemies on the other side of the hall should twist and turn my remarks, that I am in favour of proper foreign aid commensurate with Canada's responsibilities as a nation of the free world; but I believe the horse should go before the cart, and that charity begins at home, in one's own kitchen.
Our municipalities care for fundamental and basic needs; education, police, water, streets, sewerage, electric power, recreation, slum clearance and charity-a very important function of municipal governments today-to mention only a few. To my mind these needs and these functions must be fulfilled and met first, not last. These are basic, primary, fundamental needs which to an ever-increasing degree, the federal government is denying to our people because of its policy of refusing to assist adequately our municipal bodies.
I was astonished to note the figures tabled in the house recently by the Secretary of State for External Affairs regarding financial assistance for various projects which this government is giving outright to foreign countries; while it is in the same breath denying the very same kind of projects to our own people in New Brunswick, for instance; and to the people who live within the confines of our municipal governments. In the past very few years, Canada has given or lent- mostly given-$4,044,200,000 to foreign countries. Of this amount reconstruction loans totalled $1,767,200,000, and most of these loans are still outstanding. Military relief took up $105,200,000. United Nations agencies received $215,100,000. The Colombo plan got $162,300,000 outright, much of which was for the development of hydroelectric power. And this at a time when Canada's government refused a loan of $46 million to develop hydroelectric power at Beechwood, New Brunswick, a loan which my province would have fully repaid, for our people pay their way, with interest, with certainty and on the due dates. To international organizations

Don't forget the Prince of Liechtenstein.

Most of this money was in outright gifts. In the face of these facts, can there be a legitimate excuse by this government for its de facto policy of no help and no assistance to our municipal bodies? I was delighted to hear the Prime Minister the other day agree with me and all the other members on this side of the house in his admission that the government had, in effect, permitted the maritime provinces to become economically speaking and development-wise, the forgotten provinces of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the government's confession should have included as well its neglect of our municipal bodies. I admire the spirit of contrition on the part of the government in their admission of guilt, for by logical implication the Prime Minister's statement was precisely an admission or confession of guilt for so misgoverning the affairs of this country that our Atlantic provinces flounder in the sea of Liberal indifference and neglect while the government sits, and has been sitting idly by on the fence, twiddling its thumbs.
The Prime Minister now asks for proposals and suggestions. I ask what happened to the proposals we made for Beechwood. I ask what assurance we have that our future proposals will not meet the same sorry fate that has been met by the proposals we have been making to this house and to this government for the past 20 years. Let us not lose sight of the forest for the trees. If the Prime Minister thinks he can sway a few stray votes in the coming election in New Brunswick by suggesting that proposals be made to the government, he and his government are mistaken. Since 1952 New Brunswick and the four Atlantic provinces have been making proposals, demands and suggestions-lifesaving proposals-basically required for the progress of New Brunswick and therefore of Canada as a whole, proposals backed by facts and figures, sound and solid.
What happened? Nothing happened. What happened to the proposals, suggestions and demands on behalf of our municipalities made by the premier of my province at the last interprovincial conference? What happened to the proposal for Beechwood? What happened to the proposal and demand to build the Chignecto canal? What happened to our proposal and demand that you quit killing us in the maritimes with your choking

Where were you last
Friday?

What happened to our proposal that you pay the cost of the trans-Canada highway in New Brunswick? I ask this question: Whom is the government trying to fool when it asks for proposals? Since 1952 the government of my province has been making proposals; and scarcely a month goes by but that a proposal is made. But every time a proposal is made it meets the same sorry fate of indifference and neglect. Never have so many proposals been turned down so consistently by the same tired crew that runs this country.
I mention these facts to provide a background for my proposals in connection with financial assistance to our municipalities. Let no one ever try to tell this house that this government did not receive our proposals and suggestions. The government should tell the truth and say that it has been, is and will continue to be too lazy to put our proposals and suggestions into operation and to grant our legitimate rights and requests.
At the time of confederation the sources of taxation were limited almost entirely to taxes on real property. The municipalities obtained their fair share for the functions they had to accomplish and perform at that time. But today, nearly a century later, the real sources of taxation have been gathered unto the federal government, which has not given to the municipalities their fair share commensurate with their duties.
Municipalities are prevented, prohibited and stopped from fulfilling their functions and duties. Let me give you an example. Three hospitals in my riding of Restigouche-Madawaska are unable to collect 40 per cent of their accounts receivable. Forty per cent of all hospital accounts in my riding come from charity cases, and the legal responsibility for these bills must fall on the municipality. They readily admit and are willing to accept their legal responsibility, but in Restigouche county alone it would require the entire annual budget to take care of the charity cases connected with our hospital. Our municipalities simply cannot pay for these cases. So what happens? Our hospitals are faced with the problem and are obliged to shoulder the crushing burden of subsidizing the municipalities by hundreds of thousands of dollars per year, precisely because the federal government will not give adequate assistance to the municipalities.
Another proposal voiced from every corner of this house is that federal property located
fMr. Van Horne.]

in the municipalities-the counties, cities, towns, villages, local improvement districts or, where these do not exist, within the borders of school districts-should be assessed and taxed. In the city of Edmundston and the town of Campbellton the tax rate and the tax burden are to a large extent determined and necessitated by the services required because of government property located within those two localities. In Campbellton the Canadian National Railways makes up a full third of the total valuation of the town, but not a cent in taxes is received to compensate for the services that are required because of this federal government property. Yet the services must be provided, including streets, police, water, sewers and education. Who pays? It is the hard-working small property owner who pays. Thus we are obliged to pay $700 in annual town taxes for an ordinary new house. Let the government property in the municipalities be taxed, and let the government pay its share.
Another proposal is this. Let this government make loans available to all municipalities at low interest rates. Interest rates in every municipality in the Atlantic provinces are high and represent an enormous factor in the taxes which property owners must pay. It is always the struggling property owner who gets it in the neck when it comes to municipal taxes. Let these loans be made available by adopting standard minimum requirements and by making them available for specific purposes in all municipalities.
Another proposal is to exempt municipalities from federal taxation. It is contrary to all the rules of law for any kind of government to be taxed. Remove this burden from our municipalities, and that alone would ease their difficulties and allow them to purchase their machinery and equipment without sales tax or other taxes.
Another proposal is to set up a system of effective grants for our municipalities. We merely demand that whatever, in the opinion of our municipalities, is materially desirable and possible should be made financially possible by the federal government so that the needs of our municipal bodies at all levels may be met. It is the sacred responsibility of the federal government to take the necessary steps to attain these ends. Good government is nothing more than the means to an end, and that end is fulfilling the needs and wants of our people. Today the means must be provided our municipal bodies to permit them to fulfil the functions which have been bestowed upon them by law and tradition over the years.

What is the present situation? The latest statistics I have for 1952 and 1953 show that with our small population we had 5,142 substitutes in our schools, people without any professional training at all. I ask the individual members of this house if you would like to have your child sitting on a bench in front of one of those so-called teachers. Those two problems, the building of schools and the maintenance of proper staff, are major problems. If teachers are paid sufficiently no doubt they will be trained. The result of the situation I have described is widespread irregularities or inequality of educational opportunities for children throughout different parts of the country. This problem has been solved by many provinces on a provincial basis by increasing the size of the unit of administration. There may be districts, particularly farm areas, where there is a high assessment and where the people can contribute to the education of the children of their less fortunate brethren. As far as I am concerned and as far as this group is concerned that is the ideal at which we should aim.
I maintain that some remedy should be forthcoming in the federal field. As I said before, I grant that under our constitution education is a matter for the provinces, but I submit that the federal government has a duty to see that education be not allowed to fall below a certain acceptable standard in any province. I submit that is within the competence of the federal government without any interference with the administration of education by the provincial departments.
It is well known that in certain provinces a classroom can be maintained at the expenditure of $5,000 yearly, but in certain other districts or in certain other provinces to maintain a classroom at an expenditure of $5,000 a year would require twice the sacrifice and twice the financial effort.

Our position in world affairs, our position in the world depends upon the education of our people. I think it should be pointed out, and I know it has been pointed out in this house ad nauseam, that in the matter of municipal affairs the responsibility of the provinces is paramount. Naturally we in North York are interested in this whole problem of municipal taxation. I need only quote a few figures to show why it is a matter of such great importance in my riding. For example, the building permits in 1955 amounted to $78,504,000. Permits this year from January 1 to March 31 are up from $10,965,000 to $13,760,000. Furthermore, 3,940 houses were erected in North York in 1955 and the rate has been going up every year so that for the seventh year in a row more houses have been built in North York than have been built in any other part of Canada.
That fact, of course, points up one thing and one thing only, Mr. Speaker. If there is any municipality in this country which needs some assistance from senior governments it is the township of North York. But, as I say, it is primarily something that comes within the ambit or under the jurisdiction of the provinces concerned.
I am going to take advantage for a few minutes this afternoon of the opportunity of pointing out where I think both the federal

government and the provincial governments can assist, keeping in mind all the time that it is primarily the province of Ontario to which the municipalities in Ontario should look.
The township of North York municipal council has requested me to point out in this house that they are of opinion that this grant on. the 2 per cent assessment should be revised, and that the municipality should receive grants on crown lands notwithstanding the fact that they do not have crown lands comprising 2 per cent of their assessment. From the opinions I have received this restriction would seem to be anachronistic and illogical. It is a hangover from the days when the crown could do no wrong. I think it would be desirable at an early date, if possible, to have this restriction abolished.
I have only one other thing to say about the federal government in connection with municipal affairs and that is that it is the feeling of the township of North York, and I suppose that of other municipalities, that they are not consulted sufficiently in the whole area of planning. For example, when Downs-view airport was extended and one of the streets was cut off, no notice was given to the township of this action until one of the councillors-actually he was the reeve at the time-tried to go along the street and was prevented from doing so by the Department of National Defence. If the federal government could consult with the municipalities in the whole general area of planning-for example, in the extensions of airports which are so important in my riding-it would certainly be desirable.
I now come to this matter of the provincial governments and municipal taxation. It is my submission that the present government in Ontario can deal with the matter in two ways. One way is to distribute some of its surplus to the municipalities in the form of grants. The second way is to revise the whole basis of municipal taxation.
I shall deal with the first matter first. As I understand it, the Ontario government last year had a surplus of $50 million. It is my further understanding that of this $50 million surplus, $30 million was put into a highway reserve fund. If those moneys had been paid to the municipalities in the form of educational grants I do not think we would hear this continued cry from Queen's Park that they are not getting enough money from the federal government.
A select committee of the Ontario legislature decided that toll roads would have to be instituted, and so on. For example, on No. 401 highway the daily increase in traffic was from 67509-219i

I think this committee has finally come around to the point of view that we certainly need toll roads in Ontario. In view of the prodigious amounts of money being expended on roads throughout Ontario, it would seem to me that toll roads might be the answer. I would think that if the government of Ontario would look into the matter of toll roads and implement some legislation in that connection, then they could turn over some of these badly needed moneys to education instead of to highways. Last year the Ontario government spent more money on highways and public works than on education. It is, therefore, a moot point as to whether or not the provincial government has to increase taxes. It would seem to me that if they were to distribute moneys as they should, the people of Ontario would have education paid for by means of grants from the provincial government.
My second point, Mr. Speaker, is this. I submit that if the grants for educational purposes are not sufficiently great, then the whole basis of municipal taxation should be changed. The municipal act in Ontario was originally passed in 1837, I believe, under the Baldwin-Lafontaine administration, which of course preceded confederation. I am informed that the last revision of any importance was made in the year 1911. The municipalities in Ontario have very restricted rights of taxation. For example, they can levy a tax on realty; they can levy a poll tax and they have certain licensing powers. They have practically no other taxing powers.
Now of course, Mr. Speaker, with the tremendous growth in housing and the consequent development of schools, the realty tax payer in Ontario has been burdened tremendously. In my municipality of North York 55 per cent of the tax dollar goes to education and 45 per cent covers all the other municipal services. It would appear to me that the whole basic concept of taxation must be changed to meet the real problems that exist at this time. It would seem to me that, from the municipal point of view, taxes might well be considered on the basis of ability to pay, like the income tax. For example, consider the position of a gentleman who lives in a lavish apartment, and compare that with the position of a man raising five children. The man living in the apartment may be a millionaire but he pays only a small part of the realty tax in his rent, whereas the man who has five or six children has to pay an abnormally high tax proportionately. If it were based on ability to pay, then the whole basic concept would be changed-

The province of British Columbia has a sales tax, then. In other words, other provinces have sales taxes and income taxes. I think Ontario should also explore that matter. I am not saying, Mr. Speaker, that there should not be a tax on property. I think it is fitting that the realty tax should cover such things as local improvements, sewers, roads and things like that. It seems to me that the realty taxpayer should not have to bear the disproportionately high educational costs which are facing the people of Ontario. I think we have come to the point where the Ontario government has to face up to this matter of municipal taxation. Last week I saw a headline in the Toronto evening Telegram to the effect that somebody advocated a march on Ottawa because of municipal taxation. I feel that is typical of the distorted thinking which is taking place now, and the propaganda being put out by the government of Ontario. The province of Ontario has to face up to this fact; it has to be realistic. The people of Canada, the people of Ontario, the people of North York and the other municipalities of metropolitan Toronto, should know that it is the Ontario government which has the first responsibility. It is my respectful submission that Ontario has failed, and is failing, to live up to its primary obligation to its citizens.

This problem which we are discussing today, Mr. Speaker, is an old one. I suppose it is true of all democratic processes that we involve ourselves in long discussion over many years before finally coming to a decision. Certainly, there has been enough discussion on this matter. There have been resolutions galore from every organization in the country, municipal and otherwise; there have been submissions made to royal commissions. I suggest that the time has come now when action should, and in fact must be taken.
The municipalities, as has been pointed out by others, and I am not going to repeat the

arguments which others have advanced, have pretty well reached a dead end street in the matter of taxation and some action must be taken. That is not to say for one moment, of course, that this government has not done some things in connection with municipalities. We have had the Municipal Grants Act, to which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) paid tribute yesterday afternoon. We can appreciate everything he said in that connection. There have been, too, certain adjustments, as he pointed out, in connection with the sales tax on goods sold to municipalities. But actually, Mr. Speaker, these are only palliatives and do not deal with the situation as it confronts many municipalities today, particularly the rural ones. Although the Municipal Grants Act has helped certain municipalities, particularly those with a large concentration of government buildings, it only applies to a limited number of communities. It does not help some communities at all. In any event the increasing burden placed upon municipalities is such that even with the assistance of that act they still cannot carry on in these modern times.
The municipality is the creature of the horse and buggy age. It was evolved at the time of confederation. Under the British North America Act the provinces were given the power of direct taxation and also the power to create municipal institutions. Time has gone by and today we are long past the horse and buggy age, yet the municipality is still acting with a tax base which was envisaged in those old days. The hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth) who just preceded me spoke for his own province-far be it from me to discuss matters affecting provinces other than my own-and suggested perhaps Ontario could amend its Municipal Act so as to give the municipalities a wider basis of taxation. I presume it is possible for a province to do that but I would be rather surprised if any provincial legislature would want to impose a sales tax if that could be avoided, or would want to impose an income tax in addition to the federal income tax.
I was rather intrigued by the suggestion that a province should impose an income tax when the government of which he is a supporter has urged that there should be an avoidance of double taxation and that taxes of that nature should be imposed only by the federal government. I cannot envisage a provincial government adopting such a measure unless it were a matter of absolute desperation.
I think the amendment which we are urging here this afternoon, and which was moved yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), is a much more practical

approach to the problem than any involved legislation such as that suggested by the hon. member for York Centre. As I have said, this government has stuck its finger in the dike and kept the water from running in, like the little boy in the story which we read many years ago but in that case there were no other holes appearing in the dike. But in this case the dike is being punctured on all sides and the municipalities are going to be submerged unless some action is taken. When the municipalities were created, as I said a moment ago, they were the creatures of the horse and buggy age. I think that is an apt description. What were the responsibilities envisaged for the municipalities at that time? They had to look after the little red country school house; they had to provide dirt roads for the horse and buggy, literally and physically; and they had some responsibility in so far as poor relief was concerned. Other than that there were very few responsibilities for the municipalities. Certainly the fathers of confederation thought and believed-and they were right, in view of the situation prevailing at that time-that that source of taxation would be enough to enable the municipalities to carry on. But today the situation has changed so rapidly that real estate is being burdened with a crushing load of taxation.
I noticed that yesterday afternoon the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) said that once every 20 years the farmlands in his constituency were virtually sold to the government. In other words, as I take it, the taxation over a period of 20 years would be equivalent to the value of the farm properties, and that is a terrific price to pay, Mr. Speaker. We realize that these problems are increasing from day to day. There is the problem of education, for instance, on which the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) made such an eloquent speech a while ago. We all know that, according to the bureau of statistics the school population of this country will increase 100 per cent between 1955 and 1960, thereby imposing a terrific burden on the municipalities. My own small town recently had to spend $200,000 in building additions to the schools, and we are now told that before 1960 they will have to expand those schools still further. It is true that we get some assistance from the provincial government, but primarily and fundamentally that burden is carried on the real estate property and on taxes on real estate. It is true that the municipality can impose licence fees and poll taxes, and some municipalities have imposed a sales tax. But they certainly are taxes which are difficult to administer and in many instances, certainly

Therefore, we bring this amendment before the house at this time because we think, as I said, the time has come when some concrete action must be taken.
In opening the debate at the beginning of this session the Prime Minister said, as reported at page 49 of Hansard:
We did not see any need to share in the normal costs of growth of provinces and municipalities.
He was speaking for the government. The trouble, Mr. Speaker, is with the word "normal". What is normal? As I said, what was envisaged by the fathers of confederation as normal is absolutely abnormal today. The cost of streets, sidewalk maintenance, the cost of police and all these other costs which are incidental to our modern twentieth century were never foreseen at all. The government says, we did not see our way clear, or did not think that we should share in the normal costs of growth. I say when they say that they are shutting their eyes to the progress which has taken place and are refusing to face the realities of this problem.
When the Minister of Finance dealt with this matter yesterday afternoon he said, well, of course, this is a vote of confidence and I believe the government should be maintained and therefore I am going to vote against the amendment. Of course, that implied that all hon. members on the other side of the house would vote against it also. I think it is possible for the government to announce that an amendment of this kind need not be taken as a vote of confidence. They could recognize the principle of this if they believe the situation is as serious as I believe it is. I think the minister would be surprised to find how many of the members on his own side of the house also recognize the seriousness of this problem, because it is a most difficult one, and particularly, as I said, those who come from rural constituencies can appreciate it much more than others. The Minister of Finance came originally from a rural community in Ontario. Certainly he must realize the seriousness of it. As with so many other problems which are confronting the government today, the minister has pulled down the blinds, put out the cat and gone to bed to sleep on it. There are some problems he can sleep on, but this one is of such a pressing nature that I do not think he can afford to do that any longer.
I do not think I would have intervened in this debate today if it were not for the fact that it is of special interest to those of us from the maritime provinces. We have had the anomalous situation of an hon. member

In looking over the briefs submitted by the organization of municipalities some time ago I was surprised to note that the three maritime provinces are the only provinces in Canada which are 100 per cent organized on a municipal basis. We were, of course, among the older provinces. Our municipalities were organized in some instances even before the provincial governments were organized. Take Ontario for instance. The brief says that slightly more than one-tenth of the area of Ontario is municipally organized and about one-tenth in Quebec, and so on and so forth with respect to the other provinces of the country. I am not sure of the basis on which those local governments are carried on in those areas which are not organized municipally. I presume there would be some basis of local taxation imposed, through the provincial government, by a local authority. The fact is that in every one of those other provinces the provincial government exercises direct responsibility all the way from 50 per cent to nine-tenths of the provinces. Certainly, so far as we are concerned, those other provinces are in a slightly different position from most of us in the maritimes. Every square foot or square mile of our province is organized within an existing municipal organization, and the municipal government is responsible for carrying on much of the expenditure.
The second reason, of course, is an obvious one. In the maritime provinces we have not had the tremendous influx of population and the great increase in values of real property which has taken place in some parts of Canada. I realize, of course, that an increase in population also brings an increase in expenditure. Municipalities are complaining of the great degree of prosperity with which they are confronted. Because of the increase in population they have had to provide serviced land. In a few years' time they may be over the hump, so to speak, but at the moment those municipalities have these pressing and urgent financial problems because of this prosperity. Nevertheless, when you do get a continually expanding population and a continual increase in real estate values and an influx of industry and all those other factors which have been attendant upon at least so many parts of Canada, it does, I suggest, make the problem of municipal taxation an easier one than it does in other provinces which have not had that situation

prevailing, or at least have had it to a very limited degree. I am not suggesting we have not had an increase in values; I am not suggesting we have not had some increase in population, but it has not been at all in keeping with the tremendously rising scale of municipal costs and therefore our municipalities are probably in a worse position than those in other parts of Canada.
In the third place, as the municipal government is the creature of the provincial government and is a legal creation by statute, dependent upon the provincial government to a certain extent for revenues, the provincial governments in the maritime provinces, as they admit themselves in their briefs, are not in a position to make the contribution to the municipal organizations which other provinces might do.
The hon. member for York Centre said a few moments ago that Ontario, out of its surplus this year-he did not say they should have, but they could have, given $50 million to the municipalities of Ontario. Certainly, no maritime province could give $50 million or one-tenth of that or any proportion of it whatsoever. It is true that they have a small surplus, yet it is because they had to starve practically their own provincial services, and they had no money left for the assistance of the municipalities on the basis which should be recognized today. As a result, in those provinces and elsewhere too, the tax on real property is increasing and increasing. The tax on the farmer is particularly onerous. The farmer's revenue has been falling during the past several years and in many cases farm values have been falling. There are many places in my own province where if it were not for the building on the farm which constitutes the home the farm could not be given away. Farm values are down and will continue to depreciate still further before we get out of the present agricultural problem with which we are confronted, and yet it is the farmer in the rural community who is carrying the burden of increasing taxation.
In my own province we have had a new act brought into effect this year which has imposed a terrific burden of taxation for education. I am not discussing the merits of it but I do know it is causing the farmers in my constituency a terrific problem. In fact it was a shock to them when they realized the increased burden of taxation they would have to meet in order to equalize the educational system throughout the province of Nova Scotia. Of course the farmers are carrying the burden in more ways than one.

I said originally that the municipality is a creature of the horse and buggy days. What is the situation? We have young men working in the city today who are establishing their homes in the country, perhaps building or renting. They are young married couples for the most part and they have two, three or four children. Those families are living in the rural municipalities which must provide schools and other services for them, and yet the revenues derived from the new homes they build are not at all in keeping with the increased costs which are confronting scores and hundreds of municipalities alongside towns and industrial areas in various parts of this country. As I say, the burden is a heavy one on the rural municipalities.
What do you do about it? The shift in taxation has been an amazing one in the last few years. There was a time when the moneys derived from the municipalities were sufficient to look after their services. Some of these figures have already been put on the record but I would like to repeat one or two of the figures to show the situation today as compared with a few years ago.
In 1930 the municipalities collected $306 million, the provinces collected only $157 million and the federal government collected $315 million, just a little more than the figure collected by the municipalities. In 1951 the revenue of the federal government had increased to $3,791 million, the revenue of the provinces increased to $918 million and the revenue of the municipalities increased to only $636 million.
In other words, the municipal revenue over the last 20 years has doubled, the provincial revenue has increased six times and the federal revenue has increased 12 times. I suggest that a substantial part of the doubling of the municipal revenue has been at the expense of the real property owners.
An argument could be made, and has been made, concerning the centralization of taxes by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) and others and I am not debating the philosophy of that at the moment. I do say, however, that to centralize the collection through the federal treasury also envisages an increased responsibility on the federal treasury for various responsibilities of government that were formerly looked after by local taxing authorities.
I said that I thought the time had come, and I know it has come, when if this government does not make a fresh approach to this problem some other government will do so because it has gone just about as far as it can possibly go.

Various suggestions have been made. The resolution which was moved by my leader yesterday suggested the abolition of the sales tax on all purchases by municipalities. The Minister of Finance said, "Well, that is going to involve tremendous administrative difficulties and if you repeal it for one person then you have to repeal it for another." He said it was a difficult task to accomplish. He shrugged his shoulders and regretted its difficulty and implied that it just could not be done.
I point out to the minister that by his own admission he has made alterations in that tax and the imposition of it. He told us yesterday that road machinery amounting to over $1,000 in value purchased by municipalities would not bear a sales tax. If it is possible to remove the sales tax on road machinery it is also possible to remove the sales tax on any machine which is bought by a municipal government.
The anomaly of the situation was pointed out by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) last night when he said that a municipality might buy a large number of machines under $1,000 in value and not receive the removal of the sales tax but if the unit purchase had been over $1,000 in value there would have been an absolute forgiveness of the sales tax.

There would not be today with rising costs, that is true, but it is all the more reason that the municipality which is faced with expenditures should be given some assistance, and this is one field in which it could be given assistance.
The minister realizes the problem and smiles benignly at the suggestion. He says: After all, the municipality is the creature of the province. We have always recognized the fact that the crown should not tax the crown and therefore you do not tax the provincial government but it is all right to tax the municipal government. I would point out that the municipality is also a creature of the crown. Whatever the legal situation might be, I say that for all practical purposes the municipality is a creature of the provincial government. The provincial government delegates certain responsibilities to the municipality.
As far as principles of taxation are concerned I would remind the minister that several years ago-I imagine the minister was a practising barrister at that time-it was a recognized principle of taxation from the year 1867 forward that judges were sacrosanct and it was impossible to impose income tax on

Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities judges because their independence must be preserved. It was constitutionally impossible to tax judges.
Well, what happened? The government of the day rightly or wrongly, and I think rightly, decided that taxation should be imposed on the judges. It was felt that the independence and integrity of the judiciary could be maintained despite the imposition of taxation. That was a fundamental principle but' it was overcome at the time. I suggest to the minister that there is no fundamental principle involved here which he cannot overcome by simply bringing in an amendment to the sales tax system during the present session, and abolishing entirely the sales tax charged on all goods sold to municipalities.
It is true that this is not going to cure the problem but at least, instead of a little boy holding a little finger in the hole in the dike, we would have a bigger boy holding a big finger in the dike and he would therefore be able to keep out a little more water.
We had an interesting situation in my own town last year. We have a post office there which was built in 1911. Two years ago the Department of Public Works decided to renovate the building and they did a remarkably good job. As a matter of fact, they did so much renovating that they spent almost $200,000 as a result of the repairs which they effected on the building. The town in which I live was able to come within the provisions of the Municipal Grants Act and we received a fairly substantial contribution from the federal treasury on that score. It would be a lot cheaper for the government if they would allow taxes to be paid on every building in a municipality rather than spending $200,000 on repairs before the town could secure any tax on it. That was the situation in our town.
There is no reason why the principle of not taxing crown property, which we recognize as a valid constitutional argument, should apply if the value of that property is less than 2 per cent of the assessment but should i not apply if the valuation is less than 2 per cent.
Then there is the suggestion made in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) and also by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) yesterday in connection with education, which constitutes probably the most vital problem confronting our municipalities today. Something will have to be done about this in the near future. It is not for me this afternoon to make concrete suggestions as to how this problem should be met, but I do say that if it is not met there will be many municipalities in this country faced with bankruptcy.
[Mr. Nowlan.J
In the past we have urged that the government should assist with education, but I doubt if that will go far enough. If we are going to centralize more and more money in the federal treasury then the time is rapidly approaching when through the medium of dominion-provincial conferences with the municipalities sitting in and consulted, some mechanism should be evolved whereby more of that money shall be made available to the provinces for direct municipal purposes. I do not see any other way in which that problem can be met.
We have carried on for more than three-quarters of a century under the old constitutional tax basis, but we have outgrown that. We have reached an absolute stalemate with respect to this problem and a solution cannot be deferred any longer. I urge the government to take this matter into consideration and to see that steps are taken whereby this fundamental section of our economy, the local governments, be given the financial means to maintain a decent standard of government which they find impossible to do today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was surprised to hear the reaction of the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth) to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight), especially when it urges federal aid to education without interference with provincial control thereof. I am satisfied that what this means is that grants would be paid by the federal authority to the provincial governments to be used as they saw fit for educational purposes. My reaction to a question such as this is to wholeheartedly support it.
This is only one of the many factors which have been brought into this discussion from time to time which indicate the plight in which municipalities find themselves today. On examining certain resolutions moved in the past having to do with education, and amendments asking for federal assistance, my analysis of the situation is that frequently financial governments or institutions have indicated that they do not desire such assistance because they fear the motive behind the proposal on the part of any federal government to assist in a particular field of education. Possibly that is why some of the educational grants which are in existence today are not used to the optimum as we would like to see them used.
I have noticed that the field of discussion has been quite broad. Reference has been made to aid to the municipalities in connection with hospitals. That in itself is art

indication of the federal government's inability to recognize that there has been a change since the time the provincial governments and the federal government reached an agreement under which the federal authority would donate $1,000 per bed toward the cost of construction of hospitals. Since that time the cost of building hospitals has increased from $5,000 to $11,000 per bed, and that in itself is indicative of the fact that the federal government in recognizing that there was such a need before is not carrying its proper proportion of responsibility at the present time.
One or two speakers have referred to civil defence, and the fact that this government has a certain responsibility in respect to assistance in the building of bridges so that the population of our cities may be evacuated. On examination I would definitely accuse this government of using the prerogative given under section 92, subsection 10, paragraph (c) of the British North America Act. The government is always ready to take advantage of that section and call certain works as being in the interests of Canada whenever it suits its convenience, but when it comes to the responsibility of financing some of these things they contend that they are not to the general advantage of Canada and therefore they should have no share in them. That in itself is indicative of the general thought in the minds of the government today. The expenditure of money is an entirely different matter and therefore the government insists that it must protect provincial rights, that it must not help them in any way because by so doing they would be invading that field. I feel as did the hon. member for Saskatoon that such assistance could be given, as it has been given in the past, without actually injuring the rights of the provinces. Certainly the amendment moved by the hon. member is quite in order and therefore I feel that we should support it.
There is one problem in my own riding which specifically illustrates how simple it is for this government to decide that it has a responsibility in some instances and not in others. I am pleased to see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in the chamber because I should like to refer specifically to the application of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. I am quite aware that this act is applicable at the present time only to the Palliser triangle, but it has been the contention of many hon. members of this house that its application should be dominion-wide. A special committee was set up to deal with this matter and it recommended that the provisions of the act be extended to 67509-220

However, the Minister of Agriculture and the government decided that they would review their responsibility in respect to this particular matter and then they said that the rights of the provinces and the municipalities under the constitution must be respected.
I must say that I am rather at a loss to understand that attitude. We have had the proposal made from time to time that this is not just a provincial responsibility, and it is recognized as such in certain sections of the country. It is contended that the provisions of the act should be applicable to all Canada, but the government still insists upon keeping its application local.
By way of an example I have here a brief submitted by the Surrey diking district, Cole-brook diking district and Mud bay diking district to the Minister of Agriculture and setting out a problem which exists in that region. Many years ago these people diked the river to the extent of their financial capabilities to rectify that particular condition. However, the population on the upper reaches has grown and the slopes have been denuded of trees and today it is found that the facilities which were built some years ago are not adequate. They made representations to the provincial government which in turn made representations to the federal government asking that the engineers and officers operating under P.F.R.A. examine into and report upon what works are necessary in order to make this district safe. These people realize that in a period of ten years they are going to be in exactly the same position as they were in 30 years ago. However, the easy way out is to say, as the Minister of Agriculture wrote to the secretary of the Surrey diking district, that this is completely under the jurisdiction of the provincial and municipal governments and the diking authorities.
This suggestion of passing the buck, but not the one that the farmers want or the people need, is not the proper way to carry on business. We feel that it is wrong for our governments to continue telling each other, "This is your responsibility. If you check that in the British North America Act, you will find your responsibility is there."
My observations in this house up to this time and the conclusions I have drawn from them would indicate that it is the responsibility of the governments to get together to establish once and for all where their responsibilities begin and where they end and where they must co-operate to the greatest extent in order to give the people of this country the answer to the problem that they have the right to expect. It is completely wrong for
