Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities us to have to read articles in our press to the effect that the farmers blame the higher-ups, while actually the people that are to blame are the government of this country or the provincial government as the case may be. Or we ourselves, because we are not ready to face the task of establishing whose right it is and whose it is not. If it is the responsibility of the federal authorities to help municipalities and to help districts within this country as such, such as in the Palliser area, that same responsibility is with us today in so far as the rest of Canada is concerned.
The hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. McLeod), some time ago, called for a national farm rehabilitation act instead of a Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. I would strongly urge this government to go into the need for an extension of that particular act.
We get all kinds of criticisms from the Liberals about what our government is doing or is pretending to do, that is, the government in British Columbia. I must say it is mostly criticism that they try to heap on it, but that government is trying to be realistic in this particular matter. They have a diking problem before them, and so they make representations, as we would naturally expect them to do, to this government. When they find it is denied them, they realize that in a period of ten years something very drastic is going to happen in that area. The fact is it will all be a lake unless something is done very soon. The responsibility rests with the province, they are told, and they have to try to find means of rectifying it. Then, when they do it, they are accused of playing politics. That has not happened in just one instance. It happens in the case of the building of bridges. Just the other day we were discussing in this house the building of bridges. We tried to find exactly what responsibility the federal government has in the building of bridges. It was quite impossible to find out exactly where this responsibility ends and where it begins in the building of bridges. I tried to ascertain from the Minister of Public Works when it was federal responsibility to do certain rock work in the Canoe pass. There again I found it was quite impossible to discover that, because certain degree of navigation entered into the question. Even though it was a navigable stream, even though these things are true, we run again into the same question of responsibility. It becomes too convenient too often to pass along the responsibility to the federal government to the provincial governments and to the municipalities themselves.
The hon. member for York Centre, in speaking, suggested that we had not exploited every means of taxation in certain provinces today,


and he pointed with some glee to the fact that the province of British Columbia had a five per cent sales tax. Certainly it has a five per cent sales tax, but it has to have that because there is no means whereby it can get the wherewithal in order to operate its government as efficiently as we expect it to, and to carry on without that at the present time. Undoubtedly it will dispose of it within a very few years, but the fact nevertheless remains that we have to recognize a specific factor here. As the hon. member for York Centre suggests, certain provinces have not dipped deep enough into the bottom of the tax barrel as yet, and so we should force them to do that so that they become practically bankrupt.
The Minister of Finance himself, discussing this particular question, in reply to the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), with regard to municipalities that might have been refused moneys by banks, had this to say, as recorded on page 3403 of Hansard. He was referring to the two federal-provincial conferences:
On both occasions when the provincial premiers were here last year and once again when they were here this year this question arose. On each occasion I told them that if they had any instances of municipal corporations not being able to borrow money for needed municipal purposes, I should be glad to investigate the reference they would make. To this date I have not been given the name of a single municipality in this country that has not been able to borrow money for its purposes. It may well be that there are some municipalities which are obliged to pay more interest than they think they should pay on money borrowed for local improvements.
I should say that the latter part of that statement is possibly the understatement of the year for the Minister of Finance to make. Certainly every municipality feels it is being charged too high a rate of interest, for obvious reasons, because we have instituted a Bank of Canada which through discount gives to the other banks money at a charge of three per cent. This money is made available to them; why not make it available at the same rate to the provincial governments, keep it out of the hands of the banks and let it work its way back into their hands, and make them quadruple it or issue 12 times or 15 times the amount of currency they would ordinarily distribute? The suggestion that the provincial government should be given the right to get this money for municipal purposes and pass it on to the municipalities, is, I think, quite sound. There would be no more currency in the country than there would be ordinarily except that, instead of the banks being used for that purpose, the municipal government would have the money at a nominal rate.
Certain provincial governments recognize their responsibilities with respect to the

municipalities. I am satisfied with what the hon. member for Peace River, my leader, had to say in respect to what they were doing in his province. I am just as satisfied that the province of British Columbia is also doing something to help its particular municipalities. Before I deal specifically with that, however, I think that we should recognize certain fundamental facts in respect to the increase of expenditure by federal, municipal and provincial governments. I find on examining the statistics that in 1945 the federal government's expenditure was some $4,527 million. In 1955 the expenditure was $4,773 million. That represents an increase of approximately 5 * 5 per cent in expenditures in that 10-year period. In 1945 the provincial government expended $384 million but that figure showed a tremendous increase to $1,505 million in 1955. In other words, the provinces increased their expenditures by 292 per cent while at the same time the federal government increased its only by 5-5 per cent. The municipalities increased their expenditures from $334 million in 1945 to $1,293 million in 1955. That represents an increase of 276 per cent in the expenditures made by municipalities in the 10-year period from 1945 to 1955. That is a tremendous increase. According to my computation, if the municipalities of this country could get money for 1 per cent less than the rate they are paying today, they would save $12,930,000; on 2 per cent the saving would amount to well over $25 million. If instead of paying, let us say, 5 per cent, they could borrow money for 3 per cent, we could save the municipalities some $25 million a year in this country.
Yesterday, in reply to some of the questions asked, I believe the minister stated that the sum total of the savings proposed by the amendment of the Conservatives would amount to something like $25 million. Later he was corrected and someone suggested $40 million. If the municipalities could have their interest rate cut by a matter of 3 per cent,- if the average rate is 6 per cent; I do not believe it is that high, but if it were 6 per cent and it were reduced to 3 per cent-they could save that $40 million by utilizing the Bank of Canada to make funds available to the provincial governments and then passing them on to the municipalities. It would be a guaranteed loan by the provincial governments themselves. The minister would still be privileged to collect his taxes on these other two items, although I would personally favour the Conservative amendment that the sales tax and the excise tax be eliminated, for that in itself would amount to only some $40 million or so.
In my discussion I said that the province of British Columbia recognized the need for
I. 1956	3457
Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities cheaper money for its municipalities and so had gone out of its way to guarantee school district debentures. In the budget speech for 1956 of the Premier of British Columbia, who was at the same time the acting minister of finance, I find the following at page 11: School Districts Debentures
On May 6,	1955,	$7,500,000 of 31 per cent
debentures-maturing annually over a period of 20 years-were sold to a syndicate headed by A. E. Ames and Co. Limited (syndicate managers) who submitted the highest bid of $100-277 for each $100 representing a cost to the seller of 3-215 per cent.
Possibly this would have been the answer as to provinces helping municipalities out in respect of costs of education, namely that they should guarantee the loans of municipalities. But I find that later in that same year the province again tried to interest financiers in taking bonds for the same purpose and guaranteed by the provincial government but they could not find any takers at that rate of interest. Therefore the government did what I think every self-respecting government should do. It used the pension funds that had accumulated and invested those savings in the purchase of bonds at that rate of interest. That action in itself helped to a marked degree the school districts in that area. That is to say, a provision was made whereby these school districts could borrow the money and make certain savings. Later in the same budget address, at pages 22 and 23, I find certain other recognition that the provincial government had given in respect of municipal grants. They were proposing to increase the rate of payment-and these proposals are now instituted-on a per capita basis to cities and towns and various municipal areas as follows:
. . . from $14 to $16 per capita to a municipality with a population up to and including 3,500 persons
from $9 to $12 per capita for the number of persons in excess of 3,500 up to 8,000 inclusive
from $5 to $8 per capita for the number of persons in excess of 8,000 but not in excess of 50,000
from $4.25 to $6.50 per capita for the number of persons in excess of 50,000
That automatically meant a large increase of some $5 million to the municipalities over and above what they had in the previous years. Comparing that with the year 1943-44, this is what we find from the figures at page 23 of this report. In 1943-44 the actual figure of the amount expended was $3,526,000. In 1956-57 it is estimated that the government will be giving to the municipalities $43,829,000. That is $40 million more than they received just 10 years ago or thereabouts.
That is an indication of the feeling of the province or the provinces. I am satisfied that certainly that one is not by itself. Every province realizes that it has a direct responsi-
3458	HOUSE OF
Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities bility to the municipalities. But in many instances because of the present tax agreement and for other reasons-such as the fact that during the war years all the services that the government and the municipalities had to maintain had fallen off badly and that they are being built up today-the fact that the federal government does not seem to want to recognize its responsibility makes it most difficult for some of these municipalities to continue operating. The provincial government in British Columbia, through the premier, just the other day recognized that further assistance was required. Hon. members might recall that many of the speeches in the housing debate had to do with aged citizens in these communities and those on a low income requiring help. On April 24 of 1956-that is this year-a proposal was made by the premier of that province whereby the provincial government plans to pay a municipal tax on the first $1,000 or $2,000 assessment of residential property for every home owner in British Columbia. That proposal in itself will certainly lighten the load of the owner of a small property. If it amounts to $1,000 a home-that is, if the assessment is $1,000-it will automatically mean that a city such as Vancouver will receive a net return of some $3,200,000 in lieu of tax collections that they would have been forced to make themselves. I think that every government in this country, be it federal, provincial or municipal, must recognize the need and must recognize what its responsibility is. Then, it should do something about it.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would say that the Conservative amendment with respect to financial assistance to municipalities is a step in the right direction but it does not go nearly far enough. The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) has taken one particular phase and accentuated it. I would agree with him that it is an important one, and I would go along with him. I would suggest, too, that the Bank of Canada be used to make funds available to the provinces at its discount rate, on the understanding those funds must be passed on to the municipalities. I did not deal with this specifically, but I would take issue with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) with respect to the fact that the purpose of the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act was to create employment. I just cannot understand any government suggesting that the purpose of an act is to give people work. My land, I cannot think of anything in the world more horrible than to say we are going to pass an act to make it possible to give work in any municipal district. The purpose of this particular act should have been rather to create public works, to build the things the people


in the area require. This reminds me of the thirties when the late prime minister, Mr. Bennett, suggested we should build a trans-Canada highway and give people a wheelbarrow and a teaspoon or something like that to keep them working. In my opinion the objective is wrong. The objective should be to build works by using the machinery that is available for that purpose.
Then, I would propose in all seriousness that a common-sense body of civic minded men and women study the whole field of municipal, provincial and federal responsibility in respect to the division of the taxation fields as they apply in Canada today.

This amendment, Mr. Speaker, both before and after the subamendment, calls attention to one of the most important and best recognized problems in the field of government financing today, namely the mounting financial problem of Canadian municipalities. It condemns the government for its failure to do any of the several things which are open to the government, and within its competence, to assist the municipalities. Two particular measures are mentioned in the amendment. The first one is to exempt municipalities and school boards from the payment of excise taxes and the 10 per cent sales tax. This aspect has been discussed sufficiently. The government recognized its duty in that respect as recently as the last session, and went a little farther towards doing complete justice to the municipalities with respect to this item.
In his remarks yesterday the minister sought to differentiate between the position of the municipality and that of the province by saying that in one case the crown was carrying on the government and in the other case it was not. He endeavoured, I think, to hide behind that legal fiction or technical objection in his approach to the relief of municipalities from sales tax. It is well known that under the federal system we have two major ranks of government. It is true that in this sphere government is carried on in the name of the crown, and in the provincial sphere as well. However, we have a third rank of government, which is the municipal range, and as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan), their responsibility emanates from the provincial government. The municipalities are sovereign in some respects, although their powers can be withdrawn. They have the right to tax, and the responsibility to tax, in exactly the same way as the other two ranks of government have. It seems to me that any effort to dodge this issue by such a fiction, that is that we have only two ranks

of government under the federal system, is not very realistic or very worthy of the minister.
Now, the other suggestion which has been discussed also to some extent in the course of this debate is that a payment equivalent to full taxes on crown property should be made to the municipalities. In Toronto, and hon. members will understand I am speaking of the municipality in which my riding lies as I am sure we all relate this matter to our own localities, there are some 25 departments of government represented by offices and buildings of greater or less extent. If one looks at the Toronto telephone directory under the government of Canada, one will find that, beginning with agriculture, which has several offices, there is the board of transport commissioners; civil service commission; customs and excise as well as income tax division; defence production; finance department; labour department and so on down to veterans affairs. All of the major departments of this government are represented and necessarily have their local offices.
It is with respect to these properties of the federal government in the cities and municipalities that these grants equivalent to proper taxes should be made. As has been very clearly demonstrated in the course of this debate, the government has recognized this responsibility with some timidity and, as one hon. member properly expressed it, in a nibbling way. I have no doubt that in due course the government will go the full way. In fact, supporters of the government today have been advocating that the government recognize this problem. I hope that when the time comes for a vote the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth) will cast his vote in accordance with the sentiments which he expressed because he clearly admitted that the government did have a responsibility to compensate the municipalities for services received in common with other taxpayers.
Those two are not the only measures which could be taken. This amendment is in general terms, with two particular measures specified, but there are many other measures I am sure which hon. members will be able to specify. They will be able to enumerate ways in which the federal government, within its competence and jurisdiction, could properly help the municipalities with their very serious and mounting financial responsibilities.
One that I call to the minister's attention as a possibility deserving very serious attention is that of exempting the residents of municipalities from payment of income tax on the money which they pay in the form of taxes to their own municipalities. The property owner and the tenant have to pay
1956	3459
Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities taxes to the municipality, and that tax which is a tax, as I say, to a government with jurisdiction in its own field, is not allowed as a deduction when that same person computes his taxable income, and the effect is that he pays income tax on the money which he has earned with which to pay his property tax so that he pays a tax on a tax. That seems to me to be a very inequitable principle of public finance wherever it occurs.
We have good precedents in other jurisdictions for the allowance of exemption from taxable income of all taxes paid to other governments in the United States, and I should like to refer briefly to their method of dealing with this situation. The taxes paid to state and local governments are generally allowed as deductions from income which is taxed by the federal government. I quote briefly from the Canadian tax foundation tax memo of March of this year. While I am using their material I should like to commend this tax foundation, which is entirely nonpartisan in its operation, which studies tax laws and their effect on a community from a scientific point of view with the idea that they shall be just and equitable and bear as x lightly as possible. They say with respect to these taxes which are exempt:
This by Canadian standards is perhaps the most unusual of the deductions available to individual taxpayers in the United States.
Approximately two-thirds of the states as well as a number of major cities levy personal income taxes and the taxpayer is entitled to deduct these taxes in calculating net income.
Other taxes levied by state and local governments are generally deductible only by the person upon whom they are imposed by the taxing statute but where such taxes are passed on to the consumer, the latter is usually permitted to deduct the tax. As a result state and local gasoline taxes, sales taxes, user taxes, property taxes-
And that is what I am speaking about.
-property taxes whether levied by a state or by a local government, are regarded as deductible.
It is true that would cost the federal treasury some money. Earlier in this session I endeavoured to get an estimate from the minister as to the amount which would be lost by the federal treasury if real property taxes were allowed as a deduction from taxable income. As I recall it, I also tried to get an estimate of the amount which would be lost if school taxes only were allowed as a deduction from taxable income; but the minister did not see fit to estimate or to hazard a guess. Perhaps it is just as well, because, as I read the debate of last night, at one stage the minister was attempting to minimize the increase in the last 10 years of the federal government's take from the people of Canada in the form of taxes, and he allowed himself a margin of from 10 per cent to 25 per cent, and later had to admit that he was $300 million on the short
3460	HOUSE OF
Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities side. In any event, all of this money which is taken from the municipal taxpayer and which is taxable in the hands of the municipal taxpayer has been paid by him to the municipal government by way of property taxes and then he has to find additional money to pay the tax on that tax. The effect is that since most city and municipal taxpayers are also income taxpayers, from 16 per cent to the upper bracket of our income taxation, which is between 80 per cent and 95 per cent-I am not just sure where it stands now because it is not a consideration for most of us-is paid twice to different governments, and yet it is not earned twice. If that is too costly a deduction, it seems to me that, in line with what has been said here about education today, the federal government might very properly consider allowing the school tax at least as a deduction from taxable income in the federal income tax field. That undoubtedly would cost some money. It would have the effect of leaving in the hands of the city taxpayers money which they do not retain now, and it would make it much easier for them to bear the burden of mounting city taxes, and there is no question that city taxes and municipal taxes generally are mounting.
This problem is one part of a broader problem which I do not propose to discuss at this time, namely, the fiscal relationships between the federal government and the provinces and, through the provinces, of course, the municipalities are affected. However, to keep the matter in perspective, I would like to state the problem as I see it; it is very neatly stated in a recent publication of the Canadian tax foundation in better words than I can pick at random. Therefore, I take the opportunity of quoting from the federal-provincial tax negotiations, an interim report, published by the Canadian Tax Foundation.
In the background are the inequalities of government financial resources which reflect the imbalances of the Canadian economy and terrain.
After dealing with these inequalities these words are said about this particular problem:
Important as are these regional disabilities a far more universal problem arises from the seamstretching strains on all provincial and municipal governments caused by a snowballing population and a booming economy. Provincial and municipal politicians, trapped between mounting requirements for essential facilities and services on one side and the impenetrable wall of federal taxation on the other,-
And I think these words are particularly apt.
-have been howling in frustrated wrath. And well they might, too, for theirs is a serious predicament. It is amply evident even to the casual observer that the stagnation of the depression and the immobility of the war period left the junior governments in poor shape to cope with the volcanic eruption of the postwar years. A decade of striving since 1945 seems only to have


revealed the magnitude of the job yet to be done. Given peace and prosperity the provinces and municipalities will henceforth bear the brunt of the cost of providing expanded government services and facilities for a rapidly growing country, whereas their revenue sources, being less elastic, will rise more slowly than those of the federal government.
That is the problem which is the subject of negotiations not yet terminated, negotiations which have been renewed every five years since the war and are a perennial problem of our federal system. This resolution suggests there is something the government can and probably should do until an interim solution to that problem is reached.
I want to add a few figures to those which have been given here. Several sets of figures have been given to show how the taxation of the federal government has risen during the past 15 or 20 years in comparison with expenditures of provincial and municipal governments. I should like to relate the tax receipts of these governments to the gross national product because, after all, that is the important thing. How much of the gross national product, the sum total of goods and services available in the country, is being taken by the respective governments? I will give figures for two periods, 1929 and 1954.
In 1929 the government of Canada took 6-4 per cent of the gross national product and the provincial and municipal governments together took 8-7 per cent, slightly more than what was taken by the government of Canada. Now, the figures for 1954 are quite different. In 1954 the government of Canada took 19 per cent of the gross national product and the municipal and provincial governments jointly took 8-5 per cent, less than half as much as was taken by the federal government.
It is true that these figures do not take into account federal transfers and the minister can properly correct them to the extent of the transfer payments which are made under our present system. The figures do illustrate very graphically and emphatically, I think, the change which the years have brought.
It has been suggested that the responsibility and need is swinging the other way apart from depression or war and perhaps the governments concerned will find a means of revising our fiscal arrangements to give effect to that when these negotiations are concluded; but in the meantime the problem remains and it is an immediate and pressing problem, one which this resolution suggests should be given attention today and not when the fiscal relations between the governments have been settled.
If any emphasis were needed to bring this matter home it is to be found in a good many

places. The Ontario government a few weeks ago in its submission to the royal commission investigating the economic future of Canada has two very emphatic paragraphs which relate the concentration of industry and population in the province to the costs of the province in carrying out its operations. The first paragraph reads as follows:
Because of the concentration of our industry and population, it costs us as a province a great deal of money to operate. There are times, with the present distribution of tax revenues, when the province is obliged to make a substantial outlay for services which earn a large federal revenue but yield a very small return to the province. Often we are faced with deciding on an expenditure to stimulate expansion and development, when in fact it does not pay us as a province to spend the money, owing to our small return from corporation and personal income taxes.
This is not a satisfactory situation. It is one of the anomalies of our tax system that the federal government derives by far the larger proportion of tax revenue from our natural resource industries though these resources are vested in the province, which is committed to very large expenditures for their conservation and development.
The premier of Ontario in the legislature on March 12, 1956, expressed the same idea a little more emphatically in these words:
I tell this house today that the federal government has deplorably failed to assess the needs of the provinces and their municipalities which are the right arm of peacetime development and expansion. They are as wrong in this as they were in the attitude of 1945 and 1950. The unfortunate part is that this matter is urgent, that our taxpayers are being overwhelmed because they are being deprived of their fair share of the revenues which come from the very production which causes our problems. That the federal government will be proved wrong again I have no doubt, but it is my hope that it will not be too late, before they find they are wrong, unfair and unjust to the provinces.
Now, making due allowances, that is a very clear and emphatic statement from the provincial point of view.
The solution of this particular problem is a pressing responsibility. Perhaps the problem of the provinces may be left to another time but I submit that this house is not justified in any such complacency.
The scale of assistance which is given by Ontario to its municipalities, for example, is perhaps worth noting. Again I say that I use my own province and city to illustrate these points and I am sure hon. members will bave equally useful examples in their own experience and from their own localities.
The assistance to municipalities, school boards and other local agencies will be $185 million, which is $21-5 million or 13 per cent more than in 1955-56. This is from the budget recently presented in the Ontario legislature which calls for an expenditure of $420 million. Of that amount $185 million is to be paid to municipalities, school boards and other local
Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities agencies. This gives point to the adjective "mounting" financial problems which appears in the resolution.
The hon. member for York Centre criticized the provincial government in its dealing with the problem of municipalities. He does not suggest any means by which it can do better than that amount. He criticizes the division of the provincial grants as between roads and education but it is apparent that the limits of taxation of the province are very nearly reached if duplication is not to occur.
I have just one other illustration of this problem. My illustration is drawn from the metropolitan budget for this year. It requires a levy of $44 million on taxpayers of which almost 68 per cent will be devoted to education and social services. In addition there are other sources of revenue amounting to approximately $30 million making up the total of metropolitan Toronto's expenditures. I shall now read an extract from an article which appeared in the press recently:
Finance commissioner G. Arthur Lascelles described the amounts for education and social services as inequitable and burdensome. The need for increased provincial financial aid in these fields is apparent, he contended.
That is the situation confronting the metropolitan council in Toronto. We have a fourth range of government, the city of Toronto council, and their problem is very similar. In their budget this year they are faced with the necessity of increasing taxes and it is due to what has been so well described here as the insufficiency of their tax resources as compared to their mounting responsibilities.
The inaction of the government in the face of these facts is the subject of this resolution. For some years the government has been developing a centralism-or an "ego-centralism" if I may coin a word-in its general approach to the local governments, and that attitude is a sufficient basis for this motion of criticism and censure. It is only one of many bases which make us question and which destroy our confidence in the government's efforts to solve the problem.

Mr. Speaker, a good deal has been said on this motion and I am going to be quite brief in my remarks in support of the amendment and the subamendment. We in this group intend to support the amendment as indicating interest and concern over this pressing problem, but in our opinion its proposals are not definitive enough. That is one reason why the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) moved a subamendment, to at least pinpoint one of the major issues surrounding this problem. In other words, we support
3462	HOUSE OF
Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities the spirit and purpose of the amendment and welcome the opportunity to discuss this problem which is of such growing importance to municipalities across this country.
Before going on with my few brief remarks may I say that I enjoyed the speech of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). I think he made a solid contribution to the debate. He did particularly well in focussing attention on the hard core of this question, which in the opinion of this group is the increasing cost of education, of maintaining the unemployed employables and of health and welfare services.
I think all of us in this group agree with him when he says that it is a thoroughly unsound principle for governments to be taxing one another. In our opinion the elimination of the excise and sales taxes would not provide any substantial or worth-while relief to municipalities, nor would the payment by the federal government of full municipal taxes on federal properties be much of a contribution to the exchequers of the municipalities. It must be remembered that a great majority of the municipalities in this dominion would not receive any extra assistance in that way. While we support the proposals as offering some minor relief to the municipalities, we in this group think they are totally inadequate in providing a solution to the problem.
We support the representations made by hon. members in support of reviving the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act. I cannot understand why the government does not revive this legislation which would permit municipalities to borrow at low interest the money necessary to undertake self-liquidating projects.
I know in some of the municipalities in the constituency which I have the honour to represent there are a number of projects which could be undertaken if money could be borrowed under the terms of that legislation. In Trail there is a necessity for the lengthening and extension of the river wall for protection against floods. An undertaking of that sort would be most expensive and could be financed by the city only under such arrangement as this act. Then there are necessary improvements to streets and the provision of required drainage in the main part of the city. I know the city of Nelson has certain public works and improvements in the form of roads and things of that sort under consideration which could be undertaken if this act were re-introduced.
My ebullient and effervescent and effusive friend-I think I am safe in terming him that-the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) suggested that our


constitution and our present financial arrangements were brought about in the horse and buggy days. I think it is the extension of communications, particularly the automobile, which has created many new problems for our municipalities. As the hon. member mentioned, there are many people living in one municipality but who are creating costs in another municipality because of the attendance of their children in school there.
I might say that I have always had a lot of trouble with my false teeth since I left the Liberal party. They seem as if they always want to fall out when I get on certain subjects. I am having difficulty just now and I apologize for the trouble 1 am having in speaking.
Other costs borne by the municipality have increased substantially because the increase in educational standards, health and welfare standards and the wider acceptance of social responsibility for the maintenance of the unemployed. But the main problem of the municipality, as stated by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, is that created by educational costs, increased health and welfare costs and the increased cost of maintaining the unemployed employables. We believe that that is the core of the situation. Those are important services which must be maintained but which cannot be maintained on an adequate basis by the municipalities if they do not receive some additional assistance from the federal and provincial governments.
I believe in orderly democratic procedure. We hear some hon. members speaking as though this government should make direct grants to the municipalities. I do not believe in that sort of thing. I believe in the continued acceptance of the established chain of responsibility from the federal government to the provincial government and from the provincial government to the municipality. In my opinion if the federal government started to tinker around with plans which meant dealing directly with the municipalities without the co-operation of the provincial governments or through the provincial governments the whole financial situation could become chaotic. I believe further in the administration of government at the lowest level of government capable of undertaking the task. I think that is how a sound democracy is maintained.
If we believe in these principles, and knowing what the problem is today, I think we will realize that it is only a financial problem. I do not mean that it is a problem which is going to be solved by crackpots or jackpots; it will have to be solved as the result of sound procedures on the part of the governments concerned. I think the members

of all governments, whether federal or provincial, should continually bring to the attention of the public the fact that no government gives anyone anything without first taking it away from the people.
It is simply a question of the scientific redistribution of the taxes collected from the people as a whole. In my opinion grants that are earmarked for educational purposes, health and welfare purposes and the maintenance of unemployed employables should be made to the municipalities through the provincial governments. To me it is simply a question of federal-provincial-municipal co-operation and agreement in the allocating of financial responsibility for the various services performed by the several levels of government.
I want to make this point because I believe that success in solving the problems of the municipalities depends upon the honesty of approach by all the governments concerned. It should be a strictly non-partisan approach. If the problem is not faced in that way by the provincial and federal governments then the municipalities are not going to be rescued from their present financial difficulties for a long time to come. I strongly urge all governments associated in dealing with this problem to face it on a strictly non-partisan basis in the interests of the people we are all trying to serve.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the great pleasure of addressing two of the hon. members in the opposition at least and you as well. At six o'clock I was referring briefly to the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act. I want to make only one more reference to it. In the cost of all projects, whether they be part of a municipal, provincial or federal spending, there should be an item of relative need having regard to other items before the taxing bodies. Municipal corporations, if subsidized in this manner, would perhaps engage in activities which they would feel they ought in fact to carry out at that time rather than later, to make sure that the subsidy limit was available. Indeed, some of our provincial premiers-and I think what they have said has been repeated in the house by opposition members-have complained of features of our offers to the provincial government as being conditional and that these imposed upon them the choice of rejecting much-desired projects or of accepting them at a time when they really otherwise would not carry them out because of their financial position. For these reasons, and bearing in mind the fact that if one subsidizes a municipality I presume one should subsidize a provincial government,-at any rate, there is no logic in doing the one and not the other- I think we ought to go back to the first principle of the Municipal Improvement's Assistance Act which was to stimulate employment at a time when public works was the recognized method of doing that. That was the reason at that time and it would still be the reason for the use of this particular statute.
The hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Michener), as I recall it-although I was not able to listen too directly to what he said- made some passing reference to the possibility of deduction of municipal taxes from federal taxes. This, I take it, was an argument that property taxes ought to be a credit on federal income tax or something of that kind. This proposal has not been brought forward in this session previously, as I recall it, although we have had it at other sessions. I have often wondered why it has been recommended because obviously it must be to the great advantage of those of our citizens who have substantial incomes. Surely the tax deduction

for income tax purposes of a person whose municipal taxes would run to $1,000 because he lived in an expensive home is of greater advantage as compared to the deduction which would be available to the modest householder whose tax would be $100, $200 or perhaps $300.
I think the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) probably made the speech that I might have made, although he came to a different conclusion than I would have come to. His criticism of the main amendment was that the real advantage to the municipal corporations is not by reason of tax exemption with regard to sales tax nor by reason of this government paying full taxes on its property but rather because of the relative advantage to be gained by municipal corporations by welfare services which are being provided by this government. If one thinks of the period we are talking about and the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act, 1938, and recalls that the amount paid by the federal government at that time to a municipal corporation was I think $20 for old age pensions and that today it is $40;-
Its income was then one-tenth as much as it is today.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
-and if you recall as well that we now pay family allowances; and if you recall as well that we offer-and the provincial governments accept-certain grants to hospitals and the like which are a great aid to municipal corporations; and if you recall as well that on the order paper, in the name of my colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) there is a motion which would provide for even greater assistance to the provinces in certain needy cases which would undoubtedly remove some of the cost of providing these services which is borne by the municipal corporation, it must be evident that this government is doing a great deal to aid municipalities.
There is little that I can add, Mr. Speaker, except to say that the question of sales tax is always being considered by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) in order to see that, first, the tax is properly based; and second, that if there are exemptions, those exemptions extend within the proper area. We shall continue to consider the sales tax from time to time.
I should also say what I said last year with respect to the Municipal Grants Act. The experience we gained as the result of paying in to these municipal corporations where the assessment was over 4 per cent of the total, was useful in deciding that we could reduce that percentage to 2 per cent.

There is no chain of command from Ottawa through the provincial governments down to the municipal corporations. On the contrary, I rejected the suggestion of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) that there ought to be direction from this house to the municipal corporations. What we have in Canada, Mr. Speaker, is a constitution which wisely divides the taxing powers between the federal government and the provincial government. snould be available in a department for several years before it might come to the attention of the minister. It might be available to senior officials in his department, and nothing might be done about it. I would support what the hon. member for Peel said a few moments ago. It is true, as the minister points out, that the section is relatively in the same wording as heretofore, to the effect that any person who makes a statement that is false in any material respect is guilty of an offence, and so on. But I suggest that the mere fact that we have been wrong, or this parliament has been wrong, in passing legislation before is no reason why we should be wrong again. I should think the Minister of Justice, with his experience in dealing with the Criminal Code and the administration of justice generally, whatever he may be constrained to say or not to say when this particularly is before the house, would feel it should be a matter of knowingly making a false statement. What is meant by a false statement? Is it an incorrect statement? There is no definition. If it means that there is something maliciously or misleadingly wrong, that is one thing, but it states here:
Any person who makes a statement . . . that is false in any material respect . . .
I suggest that that is going much further than the law should go in dealing with an offence such as this. I am sure the Minister of Justice has read the statement made by the attorney general of Nova Scotia in the legislature two weeks ago in which he deplored the action of this parliament in reversing the old doctrine. He said that in dealing with matters of that kind the common law and the old principles on which our law is based have been largely abrogated, and he suggested that this House of Commons had been more delinquent than any other parliament in that respect. Although the Nova Scotia legislature was responsible for some of the legislation, he also inferred, and I do not know how he justified it, that it was wrong in principle and something should be done about it. It is still in this section. If a man makes a loan of $500 and he uses $15 for something else, is he going to be liable to prosecution or liable to a fine of $500 a year or ten years after the loan was made? I think this section is going much further. It is part of a trend in statutory law to shift the burden of proof so that it is possible
Farm Improvement Loans Act to convict on less substantial evidence. I want to register my protest. I think the minister should reconsider it and take it up with the Department of Justice to see if some amendment, without interfering with the principle, could be incorporated in the section that would safeguard the rights of the individual for fair trial, and one which does not abrogate all the principles of criminal law and quasi-criminal law on which our courts have operated in the past.

I wanted to discuss further the point I had raised with the minister, because apparently he and I are not talking about the same point. I appreciate that, if the operation of the act is to be extended in time, then obviously all the provisions of the act have to be extended; but, if I understand the explanatory note correctly, this is not merely a provision of that nature. This is a change of law. It is a change the effect of which is to provide that a prosecution may be launched at any time within 12 months after the evidence upon which that prosecution is based has come to the attention of the minister.
According to the notes to the bill, it is an entirely new provision, not merely extending the time, which already exists; but it is adding a new provision to the act. I do not know the purpose of it. The minister has not yet been able to satisfy us that there is any purpose for it because, as I say, he has not been discussing it on the basis which I now suggest is the basis upon which it rests, and which I question.
Further, it is provided by a new proposed subsection that a document purporting to have been issued by the minister or by any person on his behalf shall be received in evidence without proof of the signature or of the official status of the person purporting to have been acting under the minister- again, a very considerable extension of the law, and a new one in so far as this act, the Farm Improvement Loans Act, is concerned. What is the reason? Is it that the government has cause to believe that there have been numbers of frauds in connection with this act in the past which they have not been able to prosecute effectively? Or have they just dreamed up some idea in accordance with some theory of their own that they are going to strike terror into the hearts of all potential wrongdoers and incidentally to discharge people from making applications for loans under this act because of the extremely stringent provisions that are now being included in the act for the first time? What is the purpose of these two new sections which are proposed to be added by this section 5? We have had absolutely no explanation of that matter.

That is exactly why we want to know why these new and unusual provisions are added. The minister has not explained that point. He has not said a word


about it. He and I may spar and duel. I will try not to be too provocative in what I have to say. If I have been provocative previously, I shall try to change my tactics. subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR NEW THREE-YEAR POOL, MAXIMUM GUARANTEE OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I will try once again. In every statute in which there must be penalties, I suggest that good draftsmanship would require a limitation of time on prosecutions under the act. We have here a statement that the minister cannot, after he comes into possession of information which would lead him to suppose that there has been a violation of the act, allow time to run indefinitely. He must launch his prosecution within 12 months. That provision I think is advantageous to the borrower. I cannot see why it is not. In this kind of statute it is not uncommon to provide that the certificate of a minister will be taken for what, after all, is a relatively minor point and one on which the prosecution would fall from the point of view of the time limit but for no other reason. In spite of what the-minister has said I suggest, with the utmost earnestness, that in this bill to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act we are introducing a new quasi-criminal principle which extends far beyond anything which now exists in the Criminal Code for a similar offence punishable on summary proceedings. We are

Farm Improvement Loans Act introducing this principle into a bill in which it has no place, and on a basis which has so far been entirely unjustified.
I am satisfied, Mr. Chairman, that we should not enact legislation of this far-reaching effect unless it has been amply justified. I refer to legislation which changes principles which have been established in the criminal law for a long time, protections and safeguards which have existed for many years. We are asked to set these aside by introducing a principle which not only runs counter to the safeguards that existed before but also asserts such a diametrically opposed principle it should not be adopted except after the most careful consideration and ample explanation. We have had no such justification. I appreciate that the Minister of Finance is considerably embarrassed because, in fact, there is no justification in practice or in experience for this proposal. There is nothing to support it except the idea of some draftsmen in the department that it might be a good idea to write it into the law. I submit, in fact I state positively, it is not a good idea in the absence of some basis of experience which shows it should be put in there.
If the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Justice could come before us and say: We have had experience with cases under the Farm Improvement Loans Act where loans have been applied for on the basis of the most fraudulent statements, but because of the complicated nature of the transaction the fraud has not come to light until long after the transaction has been closed; after all that time we find that this fraud has been perpetrated on the government and the people of Canada but because of the passage of time we have been unable to secure a conviction; in fact, we have been unable to even launch a prosecution; if they could tell us that, or anything approaching that, then they would have made a good case for the inclusion of a section such as this.
But without such a case, let us look at what we are asked to do. I think that for the record, Mr. Chairman, perhaps the new subclause should be read out:
Section 8 of the said act is further amended i>y adding thereto the following subsections:
"(3) Proceedings for an offence under this section may be commenced at any time within 12 months from the day on which evidence, sufficient in the opinion of the minister to justify prosecution for the offence, comes to his knowledge."
So, Mr. Chairman, it is not going to be just 12 months after the offence. The offence could have been committed many years ago. It is 12 months after knowledge of the alleged offence comes to light, which extends beyond the bounds of all reason the time

within which prosecutions must be brought under the ordinary provisions of the Criminal Code.
Subsection 4 is even more far-reaching. It would read as follows:
"For the purposes of subsection (3), a document purporting to have been issued by the minister or by any person purporting to be acting on his behalf, certifying as to the day on which the evidence referred to in that section came to the knowledge of the minister, shall be received in evidence as conclusive proof of such fact without proof of the signature or of the official character of the person appearing to have signed the document and without further proof."
So that you have a provision which allows some departmental official, far removed from ultimate responsibility in the matter, to launch a prosecution long after the alleged offence has taken place, long after the facts in the possession of the accused have faded from memory, long after the evidence which would otherwise have been available to the accused has been lost, long after the persons who would otherwise have been available to give evidence have moved away: in other words, long after any opportunity to the accused to defend himself has gone by. This prosecution may be launched on the basis of a document signed by such an official who, as I say, is far-removed from ultimate responsibility in the matter itself. The document purporting to be signed on behalf of the minister requires neither proof of the signature nor of the official character; that is to say the appointment of the person who is purported to sign it on behalf of the minister. Well, nothing could be more radical in the context of the ordinary safeguards of the criminal law which, after all, is designed to secure conviction of criminals but also to provide proper safeguards. Nothing could be more radical than this amendment to the criminal law in the disguise of an amendment to the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
After all, there are reasons why it is provided in the criminal law that prosecutions must be launched within a certain time, because evidence does have a habit of disappearing and accused persons are prejudiced thereby to an equal if not to a greater extent than the crown. The crown has tremendous facilities at its disposal to gather in evidence, to seek out persons who have moved away and to bring them back, facilities out of all proportion compared with those available to an accused person, a person accused 12 years perhaps after the event. It could be possible for that to happen under the provisions that we are now asked to enact. Perhaps I should emphasize that. It might be 20 years after the offence. The 12 months apply only to the time within which the prosecution must be brought after the evidence of the alleged offence has come to the

attention of the minister. That is the reason for those safeguards of those time limits in the criminal law within which prosecution must be brought. An offence of this nature under the Criminal Code, triable under the summary prosecutions section part of the code, must be brought within six months of the date of the offence. I speak subject to correction by those who are more versed in the criminal law than I; but certainly it is a time far more limited than the time which would be available here.
Here we are, sir, in this house, asked by the government to accept legislation of this nature for which not one shadow of justification has been presented to us. We are asking, as the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings pointed out, four experienced lawyers sitting on the front bench. We admit that this matter has come up somewhat by surprise for the government. Perhaps the Minister of Finance has been shocked to the same extent that we were because of the circumstances under which this matter has come before us, but he has three illustrious colleagues there who are not demanding that he himself give us the answer. My understanding is that amendments to statutes are made when there is need to correct something that is wrong, but in regard to this Farm Improvement Loans Act we have not had one bit of evidence that there has been anything seriously wrong in the functioning of the act. Is the implication being made that people who have benefited from this act in the past have taken advantage of it? Have there been a number of loan defaulters? Have there been a number of people who have made false statements on the application forms? That would seem to be implied in the type of amendment which is introduced and which provides such a stringent penalty. Unless the government is prepared to produce

If in the past legislation of this nature has been placed on our statute books, this is a good time to call a halt. The act has been on the statute books for a considerable length of time and as far as I know the section has proved equal to the problem it is supposed to meet.
Now suddenly an enlargement is placed before us in order to make it easier for the prosecution as opposed to defaulters under the act. We feel that there is no need to do that as it leaves a loophole for bad action on the part of someone who might have an evil intent some time in the future. I would not expect the Minister of Finance to misuse this particular power, but why place temptation in the way of anyone, particularly when it provides that someone may act on behalf of the minister and sign a document which would be accepted in court as evidence of the transaction. There would be no supervision on the part of the minister with regard to that. In the course of his multifarious duties he might not have time to delve into the matter and all he would know would be that there was an alleged infringement of the provisions of the act and some documents were being forwarded to the proper authorities.
Let us not make the mistake of making it too easy for someone to get someone into trouble. As the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings pointed out, this might go on for a number of years and evidence be held in abeyance as far as being complete was concerned and then revised at some time in the future in order to embarrass someone who had perhaps made an innocent mistake at some earlier time. Whatever may have been the reasons for anybody's absence, I am delighted that the Minister of Justice is in his seat, because there are certain facts I should like to bring to his attention and also to the attention of the Minister of Finance. As the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings has pointed out, by subsection 1 of the new section 8, it is provided that if there is an offence under the act the proceedings shall be heard under the summary conviction section of the Criminal Code. Section 693 of the Criminal Code provides as follows:
(1)	Except where otherwise provided by law, this part applies to proceedings as defined in this part.
(2)	No proceedings shall be instituted more than six months after the time when the subject matter of the proceedings arose.
So, by the ordinary provisions of the criminal law, proceedings cannot be brought for an offence more than six months after the offence was committed. The minister has just told the hon. member for Greenwood that he has no knowledge of whether there have been serious offences under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. If we were to be told that there had been such serious offences and that the greatest of difficulty had been found in launching prosecutions because of the time limit of six months that would ordinarily prevail, then we might be disposed to consider whether we could extend this time; but without any such information we are asked to extend the time, almost without limit. Now it may be alleged at any time after the loan has been granted that the
Farm Improvement Loans Act minister has found evidence of an offence; and then he has 12 months after that, himself or through any subordinate official in his department, to bring in prosecution.
So it must be surely a very serious matter that would warrant the departure from the ordinary six-months rule and the extension of time without limit. How serious can it be? Is an offence against the Farm Improvement Loans Act so serious, does it involve the safety and welfare of the state, that this unlimited time should be extended? May I ask the Minister of Justice, are such offences as serious as the offence of treason, for instance? The minister smiles. Of course, he would agree. That suggestion does not hold water that an offence against the Farm Improvement Loans Act would be comparable to the offence of treason. I take it the minister agrees with me, and I am sure the Minister of Finance would agree with me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR NEW THREE-YEAR POOL, MAXIMUM GUARANTEE OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: Very seldom do I agree with you.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR NEW THREE-YEAR POOL, MAXIMUM GUARANTEE OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Now let me point out that under the criminal law, for the most serious offence known to the law in so far as the safety and welfare of the state is concerned, that is, the offence of treason, the time limit in which prosecutions must be brought is three years, under section 48 of the Criminal Code, which states:
No proceedings for an offence of treason as defined by paragraph (d) of subsection (1) of section 46 shall be commenced more than three years after the time when the offence is alleged to have been committed.
It is three years in the case of treason. But by this section, not only the Minister of Justice or the Minister of Agriculture but anyone in his department, without proof of the responsibility or the authority of that person, is given the right to commence prosecution for an offence at any time, provided only that he brings the proceedings within 12 months after he says he has discovered the evidence. That time may be any time up to 20 years or even longer. So we are in the ridiculous position that without a shadow of justification we are asked to enact with all solemnity-with all this battery of legal experts opposite, not one of whom can give any justification for it-a provision in a little innocent bill to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act, which has all the implications that an offence against that act is regarded as more serious than the crime of treason. We have been asked to swallow many ridiculous things by this government, but I really do not think they will expect this house to swallow such a mockery as that.

Business of the House I am confident, therefore, that the committee will vote for the deletion of that section. Clause stands.
